newsitem.title: USA: Witness saw suspect at Olympic blast site-report.
newsitem.headline: Witness saw suspect at Olympic blast site-report.

text.p: An Atlanta architect believes a suspcious man he saw in Centennial Olympic Park before last summer's bomb blast is a suspect jailed on unrelated charges in Spokane, Washington, a newspaper reported on Tuesday.

The Spokane Spokesman-Review said the architect called the newspaper after a report that three white supremacists charged with a pair of bombings and bank robberies had emerged as possible suspects in the July 27 Olympic bombing.

The architect, who asked to remain anonymous, said he had provided the FBI earlier with a sketch of a man wearing a backpack he and his daughter saw in the park about an hour before the early-morning blast that killed a woman and injured 111 other people in Atlanta.

After seeing television reports about the suspects in Spokane, the architect, 48, said he was convinced that the man he saw was Robert Berry, 42, of Sandpoint, Idaho. "After seeing the pictures on TV today, I'm 100 percent sure that was him, Mr. Berry," he told the Spokesman-Review.
The FBI planned to interview the architect and his 25-year-old daughter Tuesday, the newspaper said. FBI agents in Atlanta declined comment.
The daughter told the newspaper she recalled seeing a "weird-looking man" as she and her family left the park about an hour before the bombing.
"I remember him well, because he kind of looked out of place," she told the newspaper. "He was walking as if he was intoxicated or stoned, staring at people."
The architect said he sent his drawing to the FBI the day of the bombing and again in December when the agency announced a $500,000 reward in the case but he never heard back.

Berry, Charles Barbee, 42, and Verne Merrell, 51, all of the Sandpoint, Idaho, area, were arrested on Oct. 8 and charged with a pair of pipe bomb attacks and bank robberies last year outside Spokane. They are to stand trial next month in federal court on charges of bank robbery, weapons possession and conspiracy.
They have refused to cooperate with federal authorities, citing their allegiance to "Yahweh," a rendering of the Hebrew term for God often used by white supremacists.

The story was published the same day that Richard Jewell, the former security guard who was once considered the prime suspect in the bombing, reached a settlement with Cable News Network over claims the news channel invaded his privacy.

Jewell's attorneys contended the news channel violated Georgia state privacy laws by posting a camera and a surveillance car outside the family apartment for about a month after a federal search of the residence on July 31.
Jewell was cleared of any involvement in the bombing in late October.
